THE PLAYER’S HANDBOOK · CUSTOM RULES

Eleven a side.
A new kind of tactics.

This is our custom Football Chess variation: a 12 × 15 pitch, four-square goals, and eleven footballers per side. Each team has one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and three pawns.

01 · Shape the play

The attacker can dribble once and move another player without the ball once, plus use a free pawn action, in any order. The defender then has one regular move or tackle plus a free pawn action, before the attacker kicks. End positioning to skip unused actions.

02 · Move like chess

Use chess movement patterns: up to ten squares without the ball, or eight when dribbling. Kings and pawns still move one square; knights make one L-shaped jump over other pieces, including while dribbling. Pawns can move forward, backward, left, or right.

03 · Keep the ball moving

Kicks follow the carrier’s kicking directions. A short pass stops at the first piece in its path; an empty target leaves a loose ball. A friendly back-pass to the king requires an immediate kick: the king cannot hold or dribble it.

04 · Pick your finish

Aim at any legal goal target in files e–h. The shooter commits the target, then the defending king may move one legal square or hold before the shot resolves. Kings and knights can enter both four-by-two goal boxes.

Move, dribble, or send the ball

ActionWhat moves?When?
Move without ballThe selected player moves. The ball stays unless the move collects it or wins a tackle.One off-ball move in attack; one regular move or tackle in defence
DribbleThe carrier and ball move together, using that piece’s movement pattern.One independent action in ordinary attacking positioning; it does not spend the off-ball move
Pass / shootThe carrier stays in place and kicks the ball. A teammate receives a pass; an empty square leaves it loose; a goal cell declares a shot.Kicking phase, kickoff, or mandatory keeper release; a goal kick must be a pass

Attacking dribble, off-ball move, and free pawn action are separate and optional, in any order. Dribble then move a teammate, or move a teammate then dribble. Each allowance is used once. The free pawn action repositions a pawn without the ball and may collect a loose ball; it cannot dribble or tackle. Every carrier, including a pawn, gets only one dribble per attacking positioning turn. Collecting your own previous pass also spends that dribble, so you cannot pass, chase, and carry again before the defender responds. Collecting another player’s loose pass can still leave your single dribble available. The defender then positions before the attacker kicks. A turnover resets all allowances for the new attacker.

Keep the attack moving

Both teams must advance the ball at least four net squares toward the opponent’s goal within three completed possession rounds, or shoot at the opponent’s goal. A round is attacking positioning, defending positioning, then the kick; the king’s forced back-pass release completes the same round. Individual player moves do not each count as a round. Progress is measured along the pitch at the end of the round, so sideways passing and moving forward then back cannot reset the count.

Four squares of net forward progress reset the checkpoint and grant three fresh rounds. The progress panel shows what remains and warns before the last round. After three rounds without enough progress or a shot, the opponent’s nearest eligible player takes an indirect free kick at the nearest free legal square to the ball. Nobody is displaced. Both teams resettle with the taker locked, then the taker passes; a direct goal is unavailable.

A change of possession or a restart clears the old count. Kickoff, protected restart positioning, and the restart kick do not spend the three-round allowance. A pass into space still counts as a round; a complete positioning round with the ball left loose also counts. A shot at the opponent’s goal resets the window, including near the goal where four more forward squares may be impossible.

Each piece has movement and kicking patterns

PieceOff-ball moveDribblePass / shoot
KingOne square in any directionOne square in any directionStraight or diagonal rays, like a queen
QueenStraight or diagonal, up to 10 squaresStraight or diagonal, up to 8 squaresStraight or diagonal rays
RookHorizontal or vertical, up to 10 squaresHorizontal or vertical, up to 8 squaresHorizontal or vertical rays
BishopDiagonal, up to 10 squaresDiagonal, up to 8 squaresDiagonal rays
KnightOne L-shaped jumpOne L-shaped jumpOne L-shaped kick
PawnOne square forward, back, left, or rightOne square forward, back, left, or rightForward, backward, left, or right rays

Movement and dribbling use the same directions, with queen, rook, and bishop dribbles capped at eight squares while their off-ball movement reaches ten. Shorter piece patterns still apply to kings, pawns, and knights. Passing and shooting have their own range: ray kicks have no ten-square cap, while a knight kicks one L-shaped jump. Long passes lose accuracy. Ordinary passes stop at the first player; knight kicks jump over intervening players. Shots can pass the defending keeper’s square because the keeper gets a reaction; other players block the shot. Only kings and knights may occupy goal areas.

Knights can enter both teams’ goal boxes. A knight scores when one L-shaped kick lands in a goal cell; for example, d14 to the upper E goal, or f14 to the upper E goal from inside the box. Its scoring chance uses the same distance, angle, and keeper model as every other piece, with no multiplier. The keeper still reacts first. A midfield knight cannot shoot directly at goal. Unreachable goal targets show “—”.

A finish depends on the whole shot

Closer shots give the keeper less time to react. A tighter shooting angle makes the target harder to hit. The keeper’s position matters along the actual shot path, from the shooter to the chosen goal target: a shot travelling farther from the keeper is harder to save.

The model combines the chance of hitting the target with the chance of beating the keeper. A longer flight lets the keeper cover more ground. Kings have their full saving reach inside their own four-by-two box; outside it, they can only make a weaker block. The blue reach area and dashed coverage line show this geometry during a shot preview.

Distance now carries a stronger accuracy penalty: shots within three squares of the goal keep their close-range accuracy, while shots beyond three squares lose accuracy increasingly quickly. Very long shots can fall to a 1% on-target chance. This distance penalty affects shots; passing uses the separate accuracy rule below.

After the defending king reacts or holds, a shot can score, be caught, be parried out, or go wide. If the keeper stops it, estimated arrival pace and the stretch needed determine whether they hold it or concede a corner. Shorter travel means a faster arrival and a greater chance of a parry; reaching away from the body also makes the ball harder to control. Slower, central stops are easier to hold. The game currently gives all shots the same launch power and uses travel distance as a proxy for arrival pace.

This handling calculation divides stopped shots into catches and corners; it does not change the shot’s overall chance of beating the keeper. “Parry if stopped” is conditional on making the stop. A long wide shot can cross a touchline or end line according to its sampled landing. A short wide shot gives a goal kick, or a corner if it was aimed toward the shooter’s own goal. Goal kicks, corners, and throw-ins all give both teams a protected positioning turn before the restart.

Offside at the moment of play

A teammate is in an offside position when they are in the opponents’ half and strictly nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent when the ball is played. All opposing pieces count, including the king; the king is not assumed to be the last defender. Level with the ball or second-last opponent is onside, as is the halfway row. The dashed line previews the current limit; “!” marks a player beyond it.

Position alone is not an offence. A player flagged at the kick is penalised when receiving, collecting, or challenging for that ball, even if they moved back onside meanwhile. A save does not clear the snapshot; an opponent’s deliberate controlled play does. “OFF” warns of an involvement that awards an indirect free kick. This grid game models involvement through playing or challenging for the ball; it does not simulate line-of-sight obstruction. There is no offside directly from a goal kick, corner, or throw-in. An offside free kick is indirect and cannot score directly.

Boundaries and restarts

An inaccurate ordinary pass longer than ten squares samples a landing around its target without clamping it to the pitch. Scatter grows with distance. Long wide shots similarly sample an extended landing. The first boundary crossed determines the restart: a touchline gives the other team a throw-in; an end line gives a goal kick when the attacker touched last, or a corner when the defender touched last. The match journal names the award.

A goal kick belongs to the defending king, placed at a free square in its own goal box. Both teams resettle first, then the king must pass into the pitch. The king stays at the restart spot during positioning and cannot dribble or shoot directly from the goal kick. Direct receipt remains exempt from offside.

Goal kicks, corners, throws, offside free kicks, and stalling free kicks all follow the same protected sequence: the team taking the restart positions first, then its opponent positions, then the restart is played. Each team may move one off-ball player and use a free pawn action, or end its positioning early. The taker stays locked in place; there is no extra dribble, and tackling is unavailable until the ball is played. For corners, throws, and indirect free kicks, the nearest eligible teammate takes the restart at the nearest free legal square. Nobody is displaced.

Throw-ins

Any piece throws along straight or diagonal lines, independently of its normal kicking pattern. A throw stops at the first player, cannot score directly, and cannot target beyond ten squares. Accuracy is 100% through five squares, then 85%, 70%, 55%, 40%, and 25% at six through ten squares. An inaccurate throw may also land outside and award a new restart. The green guide marks the safe five-square range; the blue guide marks the ten-square limit.

Passing accuracy

Passes up to ten squares have 100% accuracy. Beyond ten squares, accuracy falls by ten percentage points per additional square, to a minimum of 25%. Target previews show the current odds before you kick.

Tackles, pawns, and knights

Queen, rook, and bishop tackles can reach the opposing ball carrier up to five squares away along their usual straight or diagonal capture directions. Their off-ball movement reaches up to ten squares and their dribbling up to eight. Kings challenge one adjacent square, knights one L-shaped jump, and pawns one square on any of the four diagonals, forward or backward. After reaching the carrier, choose an allowed landing beside it; the overall start-to-landing limit remains ten squares.

A piece that can reach the opposing carrier using its tackle pattern may tackle: choose a highlighted landing square beside the carrier. Both footballers stay on the pitch. Tackles against a knight succeed 50% of the time; other legal tackles succeed 100%. The defender moves to the chosen adjacent square either way. A failed tackle leaves the knight with the ball and consumes the defender’s regular move. Pawns can tackle diagonally forward or backward using their regular action; their movement and dribbling remain one cardinal square. A free pawn action cannot tackle. Knights can still jump over defenders while dribbling.

Computer difficulty

Casual prefers forward passes and dribbles while considering possession, shooting, and tackle risk. It accounts for the progress deadline when choosing its play. Tactical looks ahead at your replies and weighs the expected outcomes of shots, passes, and risky tackles. Both levels follow the same progress rule and scoring odds. Opponent pace controls the pause between actions independently of difficulty. You can change either setting during a match.

Match conventions

Pieces are never captured. There is no check, castling, en passant, or pawn promotion. Knights kick with one L-shaped jump; other kicks follow their movement directions. Turnovers restart the sequence for the new attacking team. A goal resets the formation and gives kickoff to the conceding side. Most goals at full time wins.

In timed matches, each action has a 30-second deadline for both teams, including the computer. Selecting pieces, rotating the board, or changing settings does not refresh it. Missing the deadline awards the opponent an indirect free kick near the ball, with both teams resettling first. If the defending keeper runs out of time during a shot, it holds position and the shot resolves normally. Pausing or opening a dialog freezes both clocks. Untimed matches have no action deadline and can be ended with Finish match; timed matches finish through the match clock.

At 00:00, the decision already underway finishes before full time. A pending shot or compulsory king release must resolve. A time-wasting free kick carries a final attacking chance through the restart and one subsequent attacking round if needed; the indirect kick’s first pass alone does not end that chance. Further missed deadlines during this final chance are played automatically, so play cannot be held open indefinitely. Saved matches and Undo retain the action time and final-chance state.

Model notes

This is a custom game heuristic, tuned for play rather than calibrated to real match data or a published expected-goals fit. Shooting distance, angle, goalkeeper position, and trajectory inform its design; the probability formula and coefficients are our own.

Background: Goalkeeper positioning research ↗ · StatsBomb expected-goals factors ↗

Football rules: IFAB offside ↗ · Throw-ins ↗ · Goal kicks ↗ · Corners ↗. Grid positioning rounds, throw ranges, scatter, and action limits are custom game rules.

The shot-model coefficients, goal-box dimensions, and long-pass accuracy curve are playable defaults for this custom variation and can be revised.
